newsitem.title: CROATIA: First train crosses former Serb-Croat front line.
newsitem.headline: First train crosses former Serb-Croat front line.

text.p: Part of the Zagreb-Belgrade railway across former front lines in the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia in Croatia reopened for passenger traffic on Monday after a five-year break, railway officials said.

The breakaway region, taken over by Serbs in 1991, is now controlled by the United Nations Transitional Authority for Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES) but is due to return to Croatian government rule by mid-June.
"The train, consisting of one four-cabin wagon, moved from Vinkovci station at 2.52 p.m. (1352 gmt), 12 minutes later than scheduled," Ivan Bevandic of Croatian Railways told Reuters.

The train, the first one to cross the region since 1991, carried officials and journalists from the town of Vinkovci in government-controlled eastern Croatia to the Serb-held village of Tovarnik near the Serbian border and back.
From Tuesday, three passenger trains will run daily between Vinkovci, once an important railway hub, and Tovarnik, the last stop before Serbia, Bevandic said.

The Vinkovci-Tovarnik section of the Zagreb-Belgrade railway, which used to connect Western Europe with Greece and Turkey, had been closed since fighting broke out in Eastern Slavonia in the summer of 1991.

War erupted when a large Serb minority in Eastern Slavonia rebelled against Croatia's declaration of independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia, capturing the oil-rich region with the backing of the Yugoslav army.
Croatia last year agreed to normalise relations with rump Yugoslavia, now comprising only Serbia and Montenegro, under pressure from the West.
But little has been done since to re-establish economic and transport links between the two Balkan powers.
